subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Martha dies
moments.body: Martha, the last passenger pigeon, dies on 1 September 1914 at age ~29. The species had numbered in the billions in the early 19th century — possibly the most numerous bird ever — and was hunted to extinction within decades. Audubon described flocks 'darkening the air for days' in 1813.
moments.takeaway: The most numerous bird in North American history went extinct within a human lifetime, driven by industrial-scale hunting and habitat destruction.

moments.title: Northern white rhino's last male dies
moments.body: Sudan, the last male northern white rhino, dies on 19 March 2018. Only two females remain. The subspecies is functionally extinct. IVF efforts using preserved sperm and northern white rhino eggs are underway; the first embryos were created in 2019.
moments.takeaway: A subspecies can persist genetically (frozen cells) even after biological extinction. What 'extinction' means is becoming technically negotiable.

now.title: Extinction today
now.body: IUCN Red List recognises 900+ species as extinct since 1500. Recent vertebrate extinctions include the baiji (Yangtze river dolphin, declared functionally extinct 2006), the western black rhino (2011) and several frog species. De-extinction efforts (Colossal Biosciences working on mammoth, dodo, thylacine) are technologically real and ethically contested.
now.open_questions: Should de-extinction be pursued? Resources spent on resurrecting lost species cannot be spent on preserving extant ones.

reflection: Martha's body was packed in ice and sent to the Smithsonian, where she is on display. Her species' total population fell from billions to one. The largest population can vanish if every individual is killed.
